solutionText: An unexpected expansionary monetary shock moves Vantry down along its short-run Phillips curve (unemployment falls, inflation rises), but once expectations catch up to the higher actual inflation the SRPC shifts up and unemployment returns to the natural rate, illustrating that there is no permanent unemployment-inflation tradeoff.

parts.scoringCriteria: Full credit requires stating BOTH that the unemployment rate falls (decreases) below the natural rate of unemployment AND that the inflation rate rises (increases) above the previously expected/anticipated rate, described as a movement along the existing SRPC (not a shift of the curve). Missing either direction, or describing this as a shift of the SRPC rather than a movement along it, does not earn the point.
parts.modelResponse: In the short run, the economy moves along the existing short-run Phillips curve: the unemployment rate falls below the natural rate of unemployment, while the inflation rate rises above the previously expected rate of inflation.

parts.scoringCriteria: 1 point for correctly linking the monetary policy action to the change in unemployment: the increase in the money supply lowers the nominal interest rate, which increases interest-sensitive investment and consumption spending, increasing aggregate demand, which leads firms to increase output and hire more workers, lowering unemployment. 1 point for correctly linking the same aggregate demand increase to the change in inflation: as aggregate demand rises against a given short-run aggregate supply (or as labor and product markets tighten), the price level rises faster, raising the inflation rate above what was expected. Both the unemployment-side mechanism and the inflation-side mechanism must be present for full credit.
parts.modelResponse: The open-market purchase increases the money supply, which lowers the nominal interest rate. The lower interest rate increases interest-sensitive investment and consumption spending, which increases aggregate demand. Facing higher demand, firms expand output and hire additional workers, so the unemployment rate falls. At the same time, the surge in aggregate demand pushes against limited short-run productive capacity, so firms raise prices faster than before, and the inflation rate rises above the rate that workers and firms had expected.

parts.scoringCriteria: Full credit requires stating that once inflation expectations fully adjust upward to match the new, higher actual inflation rate, the SRPC shifts RIGHT/UPWARD (to reflect the higher expected inflation rate), AND that Vantry's unemployment rate returns to the natural rate of unemployment (i.e., ends up back on the long-run/vertical Phillips curve at the natural rate). Missing the SRPC shift direction or the return to the natural rate does not earn the point.
parts.modelResponse: As workers and firms revise their expected inflation rate upward to match the new, higher actual inflation rate, the short-run Phillips curve shifts rightward/upward (to the position consistent with the higher expected inflation). Once expectations have fully adjusted, the unemployment rate rises back to the natural rate of unemployment, so the economy returns to a point on the long-run (vertical) Phillips curve at the natural rate, but now at a permanently higher inflation rate.

parts.scoringCriteria: Full credit requires explaining that because inflation expectations eventually adjust to actual inflation, any unemployment rate below the natural rate achieved through expansionary monetary policy is only temporary; in the long run, unemployment returns to the natural rate regardless of the inflation rate, so there is no permanent (long-run) tradeoff between unemployment and inflation, and repeated attempts to hold unemployment below the natural rate result only in progressively higher, permanent inflation.
parts.modelResponse: Because workers and firms eventually adjust their inflation expectations to match actual inflation, the lower unemployment rate achieved by expansionary monetary policy is only temporary. Once expectations catch up, unemployment returns to the natural rate regardless of the inflation rate, so there is no permanent tradeoff between unemployment and inflation. If the central bank kept trying to hold unemployment below the natural rate, the only lasting result would be progressively higher inflation, not permanently lower unemployment.
